question.prompt: Bernardo chooses a three-digit positive integer \(N\) and writes both its base-\(5\) and base-\(6\) representations on a blackboard. Later LeRoy sees the two numbers Bernardo has written. Treating the two numbers as base-\(10\) integers, he adds them to obtain an integer \(S.\) For example, if \(N = 749,\) Bernardo writes the numbers \(10{,}444\) and \(3{,}245,\) and LeRoy obtains the sum \(S = 13{,}689.\) For how many choices of \(N\) are the two rightmost digits of \(S,\) in order, the same as those of \(2N?\)

solutions.explanation:
Only the last two digits of each written representation can affect the last two digits of \(S\). Let \(a\) and \(b\) be the units digits in the base-5 and base-6 representations, respectively. Then \(0\le a\le4\), \(0\le b\le5\), so \(a+b\le9\) and their addition produces no carry.

Because \(N=5q+a\) for an integer \(q\), we have \(2N=10q+2a\). Its units digit is therefore \(2a\). Matching units digits requires
\[
a+b=2a,
\]
so \(a=b=j\), where \(0\le j\le4\). Thus \(N-j\) is divisible by both 5 and 6, giving
\[
N=30k+j.
\]
The three-digit restriction is exactly \(4\le k\le33\): \(k\le3\) gives \(N\le94\), while \(k\ge34\) gives \(N\ge1020\). Every \(j=0,1,2,3,4\) works with every \(k\) in this interval as far as the units digit is concerned.

Let \(d\) and \(e\) be the tens digits in the base-5 and base-6 representations. Since
\[
N=5(6k)+j=6(5k)+j,
\]
we have
\[
d\equiv k\pmod5,\quad 0\le d\le4,
\]
\[
e\equiv-k\pmod6,\quad 0\le e\le5.
\]
The last two decimal digits of the sum are determined by \(10(d+e)+2j\), whereas \(2N=60k+2j\). Thus the tens digits match exactly when
\[
d+e\equiv6k\pmod{10}.
\]
Reducing this condition modulo 5 gives \(e\equiv0\pmod5\), so \(e\) is either 0 or 5. The condition also requires \(d+e\) to be even. Conversely, these two requirements make the difference divisible by both 5 and 2, hence by 10, so they are sufficient.

If \(e=0\), then \(k\) is a multiple of 6 and \(d\) is even. The possible \(k\)'s are
\[
6,12,18,24,30,
\]
whose remainders modulo 5 are \(1,2,3,4,0\). This gives \(k=12,24,30\).

If \(e=5\), then \(k\equiv1\pmod6\) and \(d\) is odd. The possible \(k\)'s are
\[
7,13,19,25,31,
\]
whose remainders modulo 5 are \(2,3,4,0,1\). This gives \(k=13,31\).

These cases exhaust the tens-digit condition. There are five valid values of \(k\), each allowing all five values of \(j\). Distinct pairs \((k,j)\) give distinct integers \(N\), so the answer is
\[
5\cdot5=\boxed{25},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
solutions.title: Match the units digits first, then the tens digits
